Biblical covenants converse with treaty and grant patterns in the ancient Near East while keeping divine grace and holiness at the center.
Covenant is a corporate relationship of oath, loyalty, blessing, memory, and responsibility before God.
Covenant language organizes the story of Noah, Abraham, Israel, David, and the new covenant in Christ.
After the exile, covenant identity became central to debates about purity, law, and hope.
Covenant theology draws on biblical covenant forms that intersect with Hittite suzerain treaties, Neo-Assyrian loyalty oaths, kinship obligations, and royal grants.
Covenant theology developed as a way of reading the Bible’s storyline, especially within Reformed and confessional traditions, but it is rooted in the biblical text itself.

The received book combines poetry, prose sermons, narratives, letters, headings, repeated accounts, restoration collections, nation oracles, and an appendix produced through a long compositional and textual history.
Jeremiah 31 promises a new covenant with the houses of Israel and Judah, characterized by Torah on the heart, knowledge of YHWH, and forgiveness.
Chapters 1; 2-25; 26-29; 30-33; 34-45; 46-51; and 52 provide a practical outline of Masoretic Jeremiah without settling its composition.
Jeremiah 30-33 joins healing, return, Rachel's lament, field purchase, rebuilding, replanting, Davidic hope, forgiveness, and covenant renewal without erasing prior loss.
